current_disclosures.summary: Intel released its initial Core Ultra Series 3 processors in 2025, manufactured using the new Intel 18A process technology featuring gate-all-around transistors and backside power delivery. The company expects 18A to serve future client and server CPUs, while continuing development of Intel 14A, which is designed for external customers and builds on 18A's architectural innovations.

current_disclosures.section: Overview > Our Business > Foundry > Process Technology
current_disclosures.summary: Intel 18A (HVM late 2025) is the most advanced leading-edge node, introducing RibbonFET (gate-all-around) and PowerVia (backside power delivery) technologies for improved performance and density. It is used for Intel Core Ultra Series 3 and is expected to be the key manufacturing process for future client and server CPUs, with efforts underway to establish it as a significant foundry node for government and commercial customers.

comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's server CPU portfolio includes the EPYC Series, based on x86 architecture for high-performance computing and large data centers, with the recent announcement of the 5th generation AMD EPYC family.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and AMD disclose details about their high-performance processor portfolios and recent product announcements as part of their business description, but they focus on different product lines and architectural bases. Intel's disclosure centers on the specific transistor-level innovations of the Intel 18A process node (RibbonFET and PowerVia) aimed at leading-edge performance per watt, with high-volume manufacturing for Panther Lake expected in 2025. In contrast, AMD's disclosure focuses on the EPYC server processor family based on x86 architecture, highlighting the announcement of the 5th generation EPYC family to expand its high-performance server CPU portfolio for enterprise and data center markets, without detailing the underlying process node transistor innovations.

sentences.text: ▪Intel 18A is our next generation leading-edge process technology and has been designed to incorporate the first high volume commercial implementation of two breakthrough technologies: gate-all-around transistors and backside power. RibbonFET, our implementation of a gate-all-around transistor, is designed to deliver faster transistor switching speeds while achieving the same drive current as multiple fins, but in a smaller footprint. PowerVia is our unique industry-first implementation of backside power delivery that is designed to optimize signal transmission by eliminating the need for power routing on the front side of the wafer. Intel 18A is offered to external foundry customers and is designed to deliver improvements in performance per watt and density scaling over Intel 3. We expect to commence high-volume manufacturing of Panther Lake, our new client family of products and our first processors on Intel 18A, in 2025.
We recently announced our 5th generation AMD EPYC family of server processors, further expanding our high-performance server CPU portfolio.

comparisons.peer_topic: DRAM production nodes and future expectations
comparisons.peer_summary: The company shipped its industry's first 1β production node in 2023, produced majority 2024 bits on 1α and 1β nodes, and expects volume shipments of the 1γ node using EUV lithography in 2025.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and Micron disclose specific timelines and technical characteristics of their next-generation manufacturing nodes expected to reach volume production in 2025. Intel describes Intel 18A as its next-generation leading-edge technology incorporating gate-all-around transistors and backside power delivery, with high-volume manufacturing for Panther Lake expected to commence in 2025. Similarly, Micron expects volume shipments in 2025 of its next-generation DRAM, the 1γ node, which will employ EUV lithography. While both highlight 2025 as a key year for launching advanced nodes, Intel focuses on general logic process innovations (transistors/power delivery) for client processors, whereas Micron focuses on lithography techniques (EUV) for memory bit density improvements.

comparisons.peer_topic: Product energy efficiency and Green500 performance
comparisons.peer_summary: NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated computing is optimized for energy efficiency and performance per watt. The company powered 24 of the top 30 most energy-efficient systems on the Green500 list, including the top supercomputer.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and NVIDIA emphasize energy efficiency and performance per watt as critical design attributes of their computing technologies. Intel states that its Intel 18A process node is designed to deliver improvements in performance per watt over Intel 3, utilizing specific transistor and power delivery innovations. NVIDIA highlights that its GPU-accelerated computing is inherently more energy efficient than traditional computing, optimized for performance per watt and throughput, evidenced by its dominance on the Green500 list. The comparison highlights a shared industry focus on efficiency metrics, but Intel attributes this to specific semiconductor process node features, while NVIDIA attributes it to architectural optimization for specific workloads.

comparisons.peer_topic: Processor architecture and AI Engine capabilities
comparisons.peer_summary: Qualcomm utilizes System-on-Chip architecture with heterogeneous computing, including Oryon and Kryo CPUs and Adreno GPUs, to enable high-performance, low-power computing. The Qualcomm AI Engine features dedicated hardware and the Hexagon NPU for high-performance on-device AI inference, supported by the AI Stack and AI Hub to simplify developer integration.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and Qualcomm describe their processor technologies in terms of enabling high performance and low-power computing through specific architectural components. Intel details how its Intel 18A process, with RibbonFET transistors and PowerVia, is designed to deliver faster switching speeds and improved performance per watt. Qualcomm describes its System-on-Chip architecture using CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs to enable high-performance and low-power computing for devices like those using Oryon and Kryo CPUs. While both focus on the synergy of hardware design for efficiency, Intel's disclosure is specific to a foundry process technology node's physical transistor innovations, whereas Qualcomm's is focused on the integration of heterogeneous computing engines within a platform architecture.
